content.title: About
content.content: The multigrain bagel with raisins is a whole‑grain, ring‑shaped bread product made from a blend of wheat, rye, oats and bran, with sweet raisins folded into the dough. It has a firm, slightly chewy crust and a soft, aromatic crumb with a hint of raisin sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and are traditionally boiled before baking.
The multigrain version contains at least five different grains, boosting fiber and micronutrient content.
Raisins not only add sweetness but also provide natural iron and potassium.
The classic ring shape ensures even heat distribution during baking.
Bagels are commonly served with cream cheese, smoked salmon, or hummus.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: The blend of whole grains supplies ample fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Grains provide slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Raisins contribute iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains and raisins are good sources of thiamine, niacin and folate, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Bagels contain very little saturated fat, making them suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bagel contains wheat and rye, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the sugar level, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Despite the whole‑grain base, bagels are relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Grains contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting grains can mitigate this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bagel as a snack, split it open and spread cream cheese, avocado, hummus or smoked salmon. It also works well as a base for sandwiches, toast toppings, and salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, keep it refrigerated (up to a week) or freeze, then toast before serving.

chicken-wing-fried-coated-from-raw.title: Chicken wing, fried, coated, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are small sections of poultry that are typically fried or baked after being coated. When made from raw product, they are dipped in batter or a dry spice mix and deep‑fried until golden and crispy, delivering a crunchy exterior and juicy interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings became a popular bar snack in the United States in the early 20th century.
The term "Buffalo wings" originates from Buffalo, NY, where they were first served with a spicy sauce.
Wings are often served with blue‑cheese dressing and celery sticks as a classic accompaniment.
In Japan, "yaki tsukura" – wings marinated in soy sauce and grilled – is a common variation.
Coating can be made from wheat flour, corn starch, or breadcrumbs, affecting crunch and flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken wings provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Wings supply iron, zinc and selenium, important for immune health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When prepared without sugary sauces, wings fit well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Enhanced satiety
items.content: The crispy coating stimulates taste receptors, making the dish more satisfying.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories and saturated fat.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Foodborne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt and sauces used in the coating can increase sodium intake.

items.title: Trans fats in oil
items.content: Reusing frying oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve wings hot, often with dipping sauces such as barbecue, hot sauce, or honey‑mustard. They are hand‑eaten, pulling the meat off the bone. Wings can be added to salads, rice bowls, or used in tacos.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw wings refrigerated at +2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked wings store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored iced latte is a cold coffee beverage made with espresso, chilled milk, and a flavored syrup (such as vanilla, caramel, or hazelnut). It is served over ice and offers a smooth, creamy taste with the distinct aroma of the chosen flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Iced latte originated in Japan in the 1990s as a adaptation of the classic latte for hot climates.
Flavor syrups are often made from sugar, water, and natural extracts, though artificial flavors are also common.
The coffee in an iced latte is usually brewed as cold brew or quickly cooled espresso to preserve aroma.
Popular flavors include vanilla, caramel, mint, coconut, and pumpkin.
In some countries the drink is topped with whipped cream or a sprinkle of cinnamon.

items.title: Caffeine boost
items.content: Espresso provides caffeine, which can increase alertness and improve concentration.

items.title: Antioxidant source
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals in the body.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine may slightly raise metabolic rate and aid calorie burning.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: Chilled milk supplies calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The majority of the drink is water and ice, contributing to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine consumption.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored syrups often contain high amounts of sugar, increasing calories and affecting blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Milk can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant; plant‑based milks are viable alternatives.

items.title: Coffee acidity
items.content: The acidity of coffee may irritate the stomach of people with acid reflux or gastritis.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve the iced latte in tall glasses over ice, add a splash of cream or a dusting of cinnamon if desired. Plant‑based milks and sugar‑free syrups can be used to lower calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared beverage should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 24 hours. Syrups store best in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool place, and milk should remain refrigerated until its use‑by date.

egg-sandwich-on-english-muffin-with-baco.title: Egg sandwich on English muffin with bacon

content.title: About
content.content: The egg sandwich on an English muffin with bacon is a quick, hearty breakfast. A toasted muffin half is topped with crispy bacon, a soft egg (fried or poached), and often cheese, lettuce, and a sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The English muffin originated in the US in the early 1900s and quickly became a breakfast staple.
Egg and bacon together have been a classic American breakfast combo for over a century.
Bacon is usually cooked to a crisp to add a crunchy texture contrast.
Variations may include avocado, tomato, spinach, or hot sauce for extra flavor.
The sandwich is portable – it fits in a paper wrapper and holds together well.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Eggs and bacon provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are rich in B12 and riboflavin, while bacon supplies niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Both egg and bacon contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium (when cheese is added)
items.content: Adding cheese boosts calcium content, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the muffin combined with fats from the bacon provide a quick energy source.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Bacon is high in saturated fat, so the sandwich should be eaten in moderation, especially for heart‑health concerns.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Bacon is often salty; people with hypertension should watch their salt intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs should avoid this product.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑dense (about 350‑450 kcal), so portion control matters within a daily diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is best eaten by hand, split in half if desired. Pair it with fruit, yogurt, or fresh juice for a more balanced breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Ideally consume the sandwich fresh. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic wrap. Reheat in a toaster or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Liqueur is an alcoholic beverage made by infusing, flavoring, and sweetening a base spirit with a variety of ingredients such as fruits, herbs, spices, nuts, and other aromatic compounds. Its alcohol by volume typically ranges from 15 % to 55 %.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest liqueurs were produced in ancient Egypt, where a honey‑wine infusion was used.
The word “liqueur” comes from the French “liqueur,” meaning “solution.”
Classic Italian amaro is a bitter herbal liqueur often served as a digestif.
In many countries liqueurs are classified as “spirit drinks with additives,” not as “dessert wines.”
Liqueurs are widely used in cooking, for sauces, desserts, and marinades.

items.title: Antioxidant components
items.content: Herbal and fruit extracts in liqueurs can provide polyphenols with antioxidant activity.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Bitter liqueurs (e.g., amaro) stimulate gastric secretions, supporting digestion.

items.title: Thermal effect
items.content: Moderate consumption of high‑proof liqueurs creates a warming sensation, sometimes used in traditional remedies for colds.

items.title: High alcohol content
items.content: Liqueurs can contain up to 55 % alcohol; excessive intake leads to intoxication and long‑term health issues.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some flavorings (e.g., nuts, shellfish) may trigger allergies.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol in liqueurs can amplify the effects of sedatives and antihypertensive drugs.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most liqueurs are sweetened, which can be problematic for people with diabetes or weight concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liqueur is typically served in small glasses (30–50 ml) as a digestif after meals, in cocktails, or as an aromatic addition to desserts. It can be drizzled over ice cream, mixed into sauces, or used in culinary recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep liqueur in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight. At temperatures above 20 °C the aroma may change over time, and opened bottles can undergo oxidative degradation.

liver-beef-or-calves-and-onions.title: Beef or Calf Liver with Onions

content.title: About
content.content: Beef or calf liver is a highly nutritious organ meat rich in vitamins and minerals. Combined with onions, which add a sweet‑savory flavor, the dish is a staple in many traditional cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Liver is one of the most concentrated food sources of vitamin A.
Calf liver is generally more tender and lighter in color than mature beef liver.
Onions contain sulfur compounds that enhance iron absorption from liver.
In Russian cuisine liver with onions is often pan‑fried and finished with sour cream.
Liver can be used in pâtés, terrines, soups, and meat fillings.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The heme iron in liver is highly bioavailable and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: High in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A promotes healthy vision, immune response, and skin.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides quality protein
items.content: Liver supplies complete animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High vitamin A content
items.content: Excessive liver consumption can lead to hypervitaminosis A, particularly in children and pregnant women.

items.title: Cholesterol level
items.content: Liver contains notable cholesterol; individuals with hypercholesterolemia should moderate intake.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: Liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Onion allergy
items.content: Some people are allergic to onions, which may cause mild to severe reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice liver into 1–2 cm pieces, lightly coat with flour and quickly sauté with sliced onions until golden. It can also be braised with onions and carrots, made into pâté, or added to stews. Serve with mashed potatoes, buckwheat, or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh liver refrigerated at 0–2 °C, wrapped in plastic, and use within 2 days. Frozen liver can be stored at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for an off‑odor; a sour smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Non‑alcoholic Pina Colada is a refreshing tropical drink made from pineapple juice, coconut cream, and ice. It retains the sweet‑fruity flavor of the classic cocktail while containing no alcoholic ingredients, making it suitable for children and those who avoid alcohol.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pina Colada was officially declared the national drink of Puerto Rico in 1978.
Although the original recipe includes rum, the non‑alcoholic version replaces it with extra pineapple juice or coconut milk.
Coconut cream used in the drink is derived from fresh coconut flesh, not just coconut milk, giving a richer texture.
Pina Colada is often served in a highball glass garnished with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
Non‑alcoholic versions gained popularity in the United States during the 1990s as part of the health‑conscious movement.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Pineapple juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Coconut cream contains medium‑chain triglycerides that can be quickly used by the body for energy.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Bromelain, an enzyme present in pineapple, helps break down proteins and eases digestion.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The drink is mostly water and fruit juice, helping maintain proper fluid balance.

items.title: Low sugar when homemade
items.content: By controlling added sugar, you can keep the calorie count modest.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to coconut cream, which can cause skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Commercial ready‑to‑drink versions often contain added sugars, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity of pineapple
items.content: The acids in pineapple juice may irritate a sensitive stomach if consumed in excess.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Coconut cream is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for those watching weight.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve non‑alcoholic Pina Colada chilled, typically in a tall glass, garnished with a pineapple slice, cherry, or mint. A splash of fresh lime can brighten the flavor. It pairs well with light snacks, fruit salads, and seafood dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared drink in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours to preserve freshness and coconut aroma. If using pre‑made coconut cream, keep it according to package instructions, usually refrigerated after opening.

potato-baked-peel-not-eaten-with-meat.title: Potato, baked, peel not eaten, with meat

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato without the edible peel, served with meat, is a popular dish in Russian cuisine. The potato is boiled until tender, then baked to a golden crust, and the peel is removed to obtain a soft, fluffy interior. Meat such as beef, pork, or chicken, seasoned with spices, is added on top.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baking enhances the natural sweetness of potatoes through caramelization of sugars.
Potato skin contains more fiber and vitamins, but this dish intentionally discards it.
Traditionally served in colder months as a hearty lunch or dinner.
The combination of potato and meat provides a complete set of carbs and proteins.
In Russia, baked potatoes are often accompanied by sour cream and fresh herbs.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slow‑releasing energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function and improves iron absorption from the meat.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Protein from meat
items.content: Meat adds complete protein necessary for tissue repair and growth.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared correctly
items.content: Baking without excessive oil keeps saturated fat content low.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain types of meat and should exercise caution.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Over‑salting during baking can increase the risk of hypertension.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor bacteria, so ensure it is cooked to a safe internal temperature.

items.title: Loss of nutrients in the peel
items.content: Removing the skin reduces fiber and some vitamins, so compensate with other nutrient‑rich foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the baked potato split open, topped with sautéed meat pieces, sprinkled with herbs and seasoned with spices. Add sour cream, grated cheese, or tomato sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to an internal temperature above 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels stuffed with a seasoned ground‑meat filling (usually beef, pork, or a blend). They are served hot, drenched in a smooth cream sauce that enhances the savory filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originated in Italy, where each region has its own traditional shapes and fillings.
Meat fillings are often flavored with herbs such as basil, oregano, and parsley.
The cream sauce is typically made from heavy cream, butter, and a touch of Parmesan cheese.
Ravioli can be homemade or industrially produced; factory‑made pasta often contains extra egg for elasticity.
In Italy, ravioli are commonly served as a primo (first course) during family meals.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Calcium from the cream sauce
items.content: Cream and cheese add calcium, contributing to bone health.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the pasta and fats in the sauce provides lasting satiety.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The dish is rich in fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The cream sauce adds saturated fat, which may affect cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cream sauces are often salted; individuals with hypertension should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ravioli hot, spooned with the cream sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or toasted pine nuts. Pairs well with a light white wine or a dry rosé.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked ravioli refrigerated in an airtight container for 2‑3 days, storing the sauce separately. Freeze in sealed bags at –18 °C for longer storage; thaw in the fridge before reheating.
